title: How a Bowl of Palak Paneer Led to a $200,000 Civil Rights Settlement at a US University
excerpt: Indian PhD students Aditya Prakash and Urmi Bhattacheryya fought back after a staff complaint about their lunch smell escalated into what they called systemic racial discrimination at the University of Colorado Boulder.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Indian PhD students received $200,000 after alleging racial discrimination at the University of Colorado Boulder.
  • The conflict began over a complaint about the smell of palak paneer in a shared microwave.
  • Retaliation included removal from teaching roles and withholding Master's degrees from the students.
  • The university settled but permanently barred the couple from future enrollment or employment.
  • The case highlights cultural discrimination faced by Indian students in the U.S. academic environment.
  • Two Indian PhD students, Aditya Prakash and Urmi Bhattacheryya, won a $200,000 settlement from the University of Colorado Boulder after filing a federal civil rights lawsuit alleging racial discrimination.
  • The dispute began in September 2023 when a staff member objected to the smell of palak paneer being reheated in a shared microwave, telling Prakash not to use the facility.
  • What followed, the couple alleged, was a pattern of escalating retaliation — accusations of making colleagues feel "unsafe," removal from a teaching assistant role, and the withholding of their Master's degrees.
  • The university paid $200,000, conferred their degrees, but permanently barred both from future enrolment or employment. The couple has since returned to India.

A Microwave Complaint Turns Into a Federal Case

On September 5, 2023, Aditya Prakash was doing something unremarkable: heating his lunch in a shared departmental microwave at the University of Colorado Boulder's Anthropology Department. The lunch was palak paneer — pureed spinach with paneer, one of northern India's most common dishes.

A staff member approached and complained about the "pungent" smell. She told him not to use the microwave for his food. Prakash, by his own account, didn't lose his composure. "It's just food. I'm heating and leaving," he told her.

That exchange, the couple would later argue in federal court, was not the end of a disagreement about kitchen etiquette. It was the beginning of something far more damaging.

Retaliation Spirals

According to the lawsuit filed in the US District Court for the District of Colorado, the university "engaged in a pattern of escalating retaliation" after Prakash raised concerns about discriminatory treatment. He was called into repeated meetings with senior faculty members, where he was told he had made the staff member "feel unsafe."

"I'm heating and leaving," he told her.</p> <p>That exchange, the couple would later argue in federal court, was not the end of a disagreement about kitchen etiquette."

His partner Urmi Bhattacheryya, also a PhD student in the department, supported him — and paid a price. She alleged she was removed from her teaching assistant role without explanation. Then came what the couple described as the final straw: the university withheld the Master's degrees that PhD students are routinely awarded along the way to their doctorates.

"The department refused to grant us Master's degrees that PhD students are awarded en route to the PhD. That's when we decided to seek legal recourse," Prakash told The Indian Express.

"There is a narrowing of empathy. Discomfort is tolerated less, especially when it comes from immigrants or people of colour."

— Urmi Bhattacheryya

Settlement and Departure

In September 2025, the University of Colorado Boulder agreed to a settlement. The terms: $200,000 paid to the couple, the conferral of their withheld Master's degrees, and a permanent bar on both students from any future enrolment or employment at the institution. The university denied any liability as part of the agreement.

By early 2026, Prakash and Bhattacheryya had returned to India permanently — their American academic careers over before they had truly begun.

Beyond Kitchen Etiquette

The case resonated far beyond the Boulder campus. For Indian students and professionals in the United States — a community that numbers in the millions — the palak paneer incident crystallised a familiar, often unspoken tension: the experience of having one's food, and by extension one's culture, treated as an intrusion.

Bhattacheryya connected the experience to a broader shift in American social dynamics. She described a climate where "racism is subtle rather than overt, yet deeply felt" and linked the hardening of attitudes to the political environment following Donald Trump's election.

The legal outcome was significant. A $200,000 settlement in a discrimination case originating from a microwave complaint sent a clear message that cultural hostility in institutional settings — even when framed as workplace etiquette — can have legal consequences.

What It Means for Indian Students Abroad

The case arrived at a time when Indian students are already reassessing the American Dream. With tightened visa policies, rising tuition costs, and an increasingly hostile immigration environment, many are looking to Europe and Canada as alternatives. The palak paneer case adds another data point to a growing body of evidence that the lived experience of Indian students in the US can involve cultural friction that goes well beyond academic challenges.

For the hundreds of thousands of Indian students currently studying at American universities, the case is both a cautionary tale and a precedent. Cultural discrimination in academic settings, the couple demonstrated, is not something to be quietly endured. It can be named, challenged, and — at least sometimes — legally addressed.
